title.en: Kinds of composition and choosing a topic

hook.en: The ISC paper offers several *composition* topics: a story, a description, an argument, a reflection, sometimes a picture. The first five minutes, spent choosing well, decide the next forty.

say.en: The ISC paper offers several composition topics: a story, a description, an argument, a reflection, sometimes a picture. The first five minutes, spent choosing well, decide the next forty. In this lesson: Recognise narrative, descriptive, argumentative, discursive and reflective topics.
Choose the topic that suits your ideas and vocabulary.
Brainstorm and select ideas before writing.

body.en: A narrative tells a story with a clear beginning, a turning point and an ending; it needs characters, a setting and a conflict. A descriptive *composition* paints a person, place or scene through the senses. An argumentative essay takes one side of an issue and proves it with reasons and examples. A discursive essay weighs both sides before reaching a balanced view. A reflective essay explores a thought, a quotation or an experience and what it means to the writer. Picture-based topics may be treated in any of these ways, as long as the link to the picture is clear.

points.en: Discursive: both sides, then a view

say.en: A narrative tells a story with a clear beginning, a turning point and an ending; it needs characters, a setting and a conflict. A descriptive composition paints a person, place or scene through the senses. An argumentative essay takes one side of an issue and proves it with reasons and examples. A discursive essay weighs both sides before reaching a balanced view. A reflective essay explores a thought, a quotation or an experience and what it means to the writer. Picture-based topics may be treated in any of these ways, as long as the link to the picture is clear. Narrative: events, conflict, resolution.
Descriptive: senses and details.
Argumentative: one side, proved.
Discursive: both sides, then a view.
Reflective: ideas and personal meaning.

title.en: On the board: choosing a topic in five minutes

say.en: Read every topic and mark the kind each one asks for.

text.en: choosing a topic in five minutes
1. Read all topics; underline the key words
2. Mark each: N (narrative), D, A, Disc, R

say.en: Test your best two topics: can you list five ideas in two minutes?

text.en: 3. Quick list of ideas for the top two topics
4. Choose the one with more and better ideas

say.en: Then plan: an opening, three or four body points in order, a closing idea.

text.en: 5. Plan: hook → points in order → strong close
Never change topic halfway: plan first

prompt.en: Sort each topic by the kind of writing it asks for.

narration.en: Sort each topic by the kind of writing it asks for.

text.en: Write a story that ends with the words "and the lights came back on."
A busy railway platform at dawn
Homework should be abolished. Do you agree?
Social media does more harm than good to teenagers. Discuss.
"Failure is the best teacher." What does this mean to you?
The day I got lost in a new city

explanation.en: Story prompts and "the day I…" are narrative; places and people are descriptive; "Do you agree?" and "Discuss" are argumentative or discursive; quotations to reflect on are reflective.

say.en: Sort each topic by the kind of writing it asks for.

body.en: Brainstorm quickly: jot down every idea, example, image or incident the topic brings to mind. Then select: keep the strongest three or four ideas, the ones you can develop with detail, and drop the rest. Arrange them in an order that builds (time order for a story, space order for a description, weakest to strongest for an argument). Originality earns credit: a fresh angle on a common topic is better than a list of the obvious points everyone will make.

points.en: A fresh angle beats the obvious

right.en: Rain hammered the bus roof as the driver switched off the engine and turned round to face us.
Before the sun clears the rooftops, the market already smells of jasmine and wet earth.
Banning phones in schools would harm the very students it claims to protect, for three clear reasons.
I used to think courage meant never being afraid; one evening on a hospital bench taught me otherwise.

explanation.en: A narrative opens in the middle of action, a description with a sensory picture, an argument with a clear position, and a reflection with a personal thought.

problem.en: Plan an argumentative essay on "Online classes can never replace a real classroom."

steps.en: Point 1: learning is social: discussion, peer help and instant doubt-clearing.
Point 2: not every home has quiet space, devices or steady internet.
Point 3 (concession): online classes help in emergencies and for recorded revision.
Close: online tools should support the classroom, not replace it.

answer.en: A clear position, three developed points with a concession, and a closing judgement.
